1. Meaning of Human Rights

  • Human Rights are the basic rights and freedoms belonging to every person simply because he or she is human.

They protect:

  • Life.
  • Liberty.
  • Equality.
  • Dignity.

They are essential for:

  • Justice.
  • Freedom.
  • Peace.
  • Human development.
  • Democratic governance.
📌 Must-Memorise

Human Rights → Life + Liberty + Equality + Dignity

2. Statutory Definition in India

Under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, Human Rights mean rights relating to:

  • Life.
  • Liberty.
  • Equality.
  • Dignity of the individual

which are:

  • Guaranteed by the Constitution.
  • Or embodied in international covenants.
  • And enforceable by courts in India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Protection of Human Rights Act → 1993

3. Nature of Human Rights

Human Rights are:

  • Universal.
  • Inherent.
  • Inalienable.
  • Indivisible.
  • Interdependent.
  • Equal.
  • Non-discriminatory.

4. Universal Nature

Human Rights belong to every person irrespective of:

  • Nationality.
  • Religion.
  • Race.
  • Caste.
  • Sex.
  • Language.
  • Social status.

5. Inherent Rights

Human Rights are:

  • Not granted merely by Government.
  • Inherent in human existence.
  • Closely connected with human dignity.

6. Inalienable Rights

Human Rights are described as inalienable because:

  • They cannot ordinarily be taken away arbitrarily.
  • Every person retains basic dignity and legal protection.

7. Indivisible and Interdependent

Civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights are interconnected.

For example:

  • Education supports employment.
  • Health supports dignity.
  • Liberty supports political participation.

8. Types of Human Rights

Human Rights may broadly be classified as:

  • Civil Rights.
  • Political Rights.
  • Economic Rights.
  • Social Rights.
  • Cultural Rights.

9. Civil Rights

Civil Rights protect:

  • Individual liberty.
  • Personal security.
  • Equality.
  • Freedom from arbitrary treatment.

10. Political Rights

Political Rights enable individuals to participate in:

  • Government.
  • Elections.
  • Public affairs

subject to applicable law.

11. Economic Rights

Economic Rights relate to:

  • Work.
  • Livelihood.
  • Social security.
  • Economic welfare.

12. Social Rights

Social Rights include interests relating to:

  • Education.
  • Healthcare.
  • Housing.
  • Social welfare.

13. Cultural Rights

Cultural Rights protect:

  • Cultural identity.
  • Language.
  • Participation in cultural life.

31. Constitutional Framework

The Constitution protects Human Rights through:

  • Fundamental Rights.
  • Directive Principles of State Policy.
  • Fundamental Duties.
  • Independent Judiciary.
  • Constitutional Remedies.

32. Fundamental Rights

Fundamental Rights protect:

  • Equality.
  • Freedom.
  • Life.
  • Religious freedom.
  • Constitutional remedies.

They are:

  • Enforceable by courts.

33. Directive Principles

Directive Principles promote:

  • Social justice.
  • Economic justice.
  • Public health.
  • Education.
  • Welfare.
  • Equal opportunity.

They are:

  • Non-justiciable.
  • Guides to State policy.

34. Fundamental Duties

Fundamental Duties encourage citizens to:

  • Respect Constitution.
  • Promote harmony.
  • Protect public property.
  • Protect environment.
  • Develop scientific temper.
  • Respect dignity of women.

35. Human Rights vs Fundamental Rights

Human Rights:

  • Universal.
  • Broader concept.
  • Internationally recognised.

Fundamental Rights:

  • Guaranteed by Indian Constitution.
  • Enforceable by Indian courts.
  • Constitute part of India's Human Rights framework.

152. Rule of Law vs Rule by Law

Rule of Law:

  • Law governs everyone equally.
  • Protects rights.
  • Limits arbitrary power.

Rule by Law:

  • Government may merely use law as an instrument of authority.
  • Justice and equality are not necessarily guaranteed.

153. Rights vs Duties

Rights:

  • Provide legal protection and freedoms.

Duties:

  • Require responsible behaviour.
  • Encourage respect for rights of others and constitutional values.

Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected

What are Human Rights? → Basic rights and freedoms belonging to every person simply because they are human.

Which four concepts define Human Rights under the Protection of Human Rights Act? → Life, Liberty, Equality and Dignity.

Which Act defines Human Rights in India? → Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.

What is the nature of Human Rights? → Universal, inherent, inalienable, indivisible, interdependent, equal and non-discriminatory.

What are the broad categories? → Civil, Political, Economic, Social and Cultural Rights.

Which medieval document is an early milestone? → Magna Carta, 1215.

When was English Bill of Rights adopted? → 1689.

American Declaration of Independence? → 1776.

French Declaration of Rights of Man and Citizen? → 1789.

UN Charter? → 1945.

What is UDHR? → Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

Who adopted it? → United Nations General Assembly.

When? → 10 December 1948.

Is UDHR a treaty? → No.

Is UDHR legally binding by itself? → No.

Why is it important? → It strongly influenced international Human Rights law and national Constitutions.

Which date is celebrated as Human Rights Day? → 10 December.

What is ICCPR? → International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights.

What is ICESCR? → International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights.

Is India a party to ICCPR and ICESCR according to the source? → Yes.

How does Indian Constitution protect Human Rights? → Fundamental Rights, DPSPs, Fundamental Duties, Independent Judiciary and Constitutional Remedies.

Are Fundamental Rights enforceable? → Yes.

Are Directive Principles directly enforceable? → No.

Which Act established NHRC and SHRCs? → Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.

What is NHRC? → National Human Rights Commission.

Is NHRC a Constitutional Body? → No.

What kind of body is it? → Statutory Body.

Where is NHRC headquarters? → New Delhi.

Who appoints NHRC Chairperson and Members? → President.

Who removes them according to statutory procedure? → President.

What can NHRC inquire into? → Human Rights violations and negligence by public servants in preventing them.

Can NHRC act suo motu? → Yes.

Can NHRC visit prisons? → Yes.

Why? → To examine living conditions, treatment and Human Rights compliance.

Does NHRC have Civil-Court-like powers? → Yes.

Can NHRC summon witnesses? → Yes.

Can it call for public records? → Yes.

Can NHRC recommend compensation? → Yes.

Can it recommend prosecution? → Yes.

Are NHRC recommendations automatically binding? → No, generally recommendatory.

What is SHRC? → State Human Rights Commission.

Who appoints SHRC Members? → Governor.

Who may establish SHRC? → State Government under the 1993 Act.

What are Human Rights Courts? → Courts designated for speedy trial of offences arising out of Human Rights violations.

Which court may be designated? → Court of Session.

What is the basic difference between NHRC and Human Rights Court? → NHRC investigates and recommends; Court conducts trial and gives judicial decision.

Name major vulnerable groups identified in the source. → Women, children, SCs, STs, Persons with Disabilities, senior citizens, minorities, prisoners and persons in custody.

Do prisoners retain Human Rights? → Yes, subject to lawful restrictions arising from imprisonment.

What are major Human Rights challenges? → Poverty, discrimination, child labour, trafficking, custodial violence, gender violence and digital privacy issues.

Which Article guarantees Equality Before Law? → Article 14.

Which Article abolishes Untouchability? → Article 17.

Which Article guarantees major freedoms? → Article 19.

Which Article gives criminal-law safeguards? → Article 20.

Which Article protects Life and Personal Liberty? → Article 21.

Which Article gives Right to Education? → Article 21A.

What age group? → 6–14 years.

Which Article gives arrest and detention safeguards? → Article 22.

Which Article prohibits trafficking and forced labour? → Article 23.

Which Article prohibits specified child labour? → Article 24.

Which Article protects freedom of religion? → Article 25.

Which Article provides Supreme Court remedy for Fundamental Rights? → Article 32.

Who called Article 32 Heart and Soul of Constitution? → Dr. B.R. Ambedkar.

Which Article gives High Courts wider writ jurisdiction? → Article 226.

Which Article provides Equal Justice and Free Legal Aid? → Article 39A.

Which Article relates to Right to Work and public assistance as a DPSP? → Article 41.

Which Article provides humane work conditions and maternity relief? → Article 42.

Which Article promotes weaker sections' educational and economic interests? → Article 46.

Which Article deals with public health? → Article 47.

Which Article deals with environment? → Article 48A.

Which case evolved Basic Structure Doctrine? → Kesavananda Bharati, 1973.

Which case held Article 21 procedure must be fair, just and reasonable? → Maneka Gandhi, 1978.

What is the Golden Triangle? → Articles 14, 19 and 21.

Which case strengthened prisoners' rights? → Sunil Batra.

Which case recognised Right to Speedy Trial? → Hussainara Khatoon, 1979.

Which case recognised Right to Livelihood? → Olga Tellis, 1985.

Which case evolved Absolute Liability? → M.C. Mehta, 1987.

Which case laid down arrest and detention guidelines? → D.K. Basu, 1997.

Which case framed workplace sexual-harassment guidelines? → Vishaka, 1997.

Which case dealt with telephone tapping and privacy? → PUCL, 1997.

Which case is associated with Right to Food? → PUCL Right to Food litigation.

Which case is associated with Police Reforms? → Prakash Singh, 2006.

Which case recognised Privacy as a Fundamental Right? → K.S. Puttaswamy, 2017.

Which case strengthened equality, dignity and autonomy in consensual same-sex relations? → Navtej Singh Johar, 2018.

Which case struck down the adultery offence? → Joseph Shine, 2018.

Which case recognised Passive Euthanasia and Living Wills? → Common Cause, 2018.

Which case dealt with internet restrictions and proportionality? → Anuradha Bhasin, 2020.

What is the easiest Human Rights memory line? → UDHR 1948 gives the international foundation; Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 creates NHRC–SHRC–Human Rights Courts; Articles 14, 19, 21, 32 and 226 form the core constitutional protection in India.
